People assume that in-house counsel read contracts from the first page, and I have never once done that. I go to the back. I read the governing law, the termination clause and the liability cap first, in that order, because those three tell me what happens on the worst day, and everything at the front is only interesting if we get to the worst day. Then I read every sentence with a modal verb in it and I mark them in two colours: one for what we owe them, one for what they owe us. It takes twenty minutes and it has saved me from signing three agreements I would still be explaining today. The thing I look hardest for is the clause that removes a duty without granting a permission, because that is the one everybody misreads, including me, twice.

I have been teaching contract drafting for eleven years, and the argument about shall is the one that makes previously calm people shout. Here is where I have landed. Shall is not evil. The problem is that a single word is being asked to do four different jobs in the same document, and no reader can tell which job it is doing without stopping to think. Must is not aggressive, it is simply unfamiliar, and unfamiliar wears off in about a week. What actually persuades a sceptical partner is not the style guide. It is opening their own contract, finding the fourth or fifth shall on the page, and asking them, out loud, whether that sentence creates a duty or describes something that will happen. Half the time they cannot answer, and that is the end of the argument.
